explanations.explanation: This feature is a subword‐level detector for proper‐name tokens—especially personal names (first or last names) and similar multiword named entities.

This feature fires on “meta-text” tokens rather than ordinary prose—i.e. URLs, file- or code-identifiers, snippets of code/markup, citation strings, unusual punctuation or foreign-script subwords and other reference/metadata elements.

This neuron fires on formatting/structural punctuation tokens—especially the Markdown‐style double-asterisk bold markers and isolated periods (as in initials, decimals, datelines, bylines, etc.) that signal metadata or emphasis boundaries.

This neuron consistently lights up on standalone “heading” or “title‐style” spans—the opening, label-like tokens of section titles, captions or document headings (e.g. article headlines, photo captions, case names, paper titles, bylines, etc.), rather than ordinary inline prose.

This feature fires on identifier‐tokens—especially short, often single-letter names (and occasionally brief field names like “score”)—whenever they’re used as placeholders in formal notation (math formulas, sub/superscripts or code), marking them out as variable symbols.

This feature detects tokens that open or label a new high-level section or block (e.g. section headers in prose or UI, code comment/license headers, class/doctype declarations, calls-to-action), marking the start of a distinct content unit.

This neuron is a “repeat” detector – it lights up when you see the same letter‐sequence or token fragment (e.g. “in,” “child,” “file,” “thiol,” “.,” etc.) appear again in the immediate context. It flags second/subsequent occurrences of an n-gram, signaling a copy/repetition of recently seen text.

This neuron is strongly signalling the onset of a content‐bearing subword (a root or affix) – in English (en-, dis-, pro-, in-, il-, etc.) or even in Russian (-ожн-) – basically flagging the first BPE/WordPiece chunk of a word or morphological component.

This neuron is picking out formal numeric identifiers in prose – most prominently four-digit years (e.g. birth/death dates, release dates) and registry-style numbers (U.S. Pat. No., category tags, patent citations). It flags those date- and ID-like digit sequences used as metadata.
